---

**On the polynomial-overhead assumption and the A/H complexity gap.**

These are two different uses, and it's worth keeping them apart in the paper.

*Polynomial overhead* is not doing any work specific to your construction — it's the standard precondition for a logical inductor to exist at all. Garrabrant's existence proof builds the market by having `MarketMaker` anticipate the budgeted supertrader (`TradingFirm`, §5.3), and assembling/running that supertrader costs polynomial overhead over the individual traders; the class must be closed under it so the aggregate stays in-class and the per-day market-clearing is computable. So closure under poly overhead is invoked exactly once for each side, inside Lemma 1 (Existence): once to get $H$ (hence $H^+$ by 4.7.2) over $\mathcal C_H$, once to get $A$ over $\mathcal C_A$. It says nothing about A-vs-H; it's a same-class condition you'd state for any single inductor.

*The gap* $\mathcal C_A\supsetneq\mathcal C_H$ does all the real work, and in exactly two places:

1. **The idealization (the more-powerful-reasoner paragraph and Lemma 1's hypothesis).** $Y_n=H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ is assumed $\mathcal C_A$-computable but is generally *not* $\mathcal C_H$-computable: A can simulate the coupled system to stage $F(n)$ within budget $\sigma(n)$, whereas H⁺ cannot shortcut to its own future credence faster than living to $F(n)$. This is what makes $D_A$ a legitimate computable deductive process (the contract $C_n$ can settle against a value A actually has by $\sigma(n)>F(n)$) — and it's the only place the gap is logically *required*.

2. **Tracking, and hence the informativeness of the advice.** Tracking ($a_n\to Y_n$) is A pricing a contract that resolves against a value it can compute with good feedback — Unbiasedness From Feedback (4.3.8) for A. The gap is what makes this *anticipatory*: A's quote tells H⁺ where it is headed before H⁺ could compute that itself. Collapse the gap ($\mathcal C_A=\mathcal C_H$) and the construction still type-checks, but A can't reach $Y_n$ any faster than H⁺ does, so the quote anticipates nothing and the "acceleration" content evaporates. So the gap is precisely the dial that converts A from a redundant peer into a useful advisor.

One distinction worth a sentence in the paper, because it's the subtle part your existing text already half-gestures at ("simulation being in $\mathcal C_A$ doesn't entail an efficient algorithm for traders"): the gap is used at the level of the *deductive process* — defining $D_A$ requires $\mathcal C_A$ to compute $Y_n$ once, to settle the contract — **not** at the level of A's *traders*, who never recompute $Y_n$ but instead learn to price $C_n$ by calibration. That's why a single hard simulation, amortized into $D_A$, suffices rather than requiring every trader to be that powerful.

And the thing the gap notably does *not* touch — worth stating once you add the pull section — is the displacement bound: when you get to Confinement, $H^+_\infty(\phi)$ is confined to $\phi$'s coherent interval regardless of how large $\mathcal C_A$ is. The gap is an efficiency/anticipation dial, not a depth dial.

Yes, the **computable online process framing can work with the proof**, but only if we are very precise about the time parameter.

The proof of Closure Under Conditioning does **not** merely require that the conditioned-on facts are true or eventually available. It requires an **e.c. deductive process** (D') producing those facts, so that the sequence of cumulative conditions

[
\psi^\circ_n=\bigwedge_{\psi\in D'_n}\psi
]

is effectively available to the trader construction. In Appendix G.8, Garrabrant et al. explicitly generalize from a fixed sentence sequence to “any e.c. (D')” and condition on the conjunction of all sentences that have appeared in (D') up to time (n). They then prove that the resulting conditional market is a logical inductor over the combined deductive process (D^\circ_n=D_n\cup D'_n), assuming the combined theory is consistent. 

So the important question is:

> Can the advisor’s realized quote stream be treated as an e.c. deductive process (D') from the perspective of the base LI construction?

If yes, Closure Under Conditioning applies. If no, it does not.

## Why “A computes it” is not by itself enough

If (A) computes quote (Q_n), but this computation is not efficiently computable in the time scale used for (H)’s logical induction, then we cannot simply plug

[
Q_1,Q_2,\ldots
]

into Theorem 4.7.2 as an efficiently computable sequence.

The proof constructs a trader (T) against the original market (P) from a hypothetical trader (T^\circ) exploiting the conditional market (P^\circ). To do this, (T) must build trades involving the cumulative condition (\psi^\circ_n). The proof’s sketch says (T) mimics (T^\circ) “in the worlds where (\psi^\circ_n) is true,” using conditional-contract-like combinations involving (\phi\wedge\psi^\circ_n).  If (\psi^\circ_n) is not efficiently obtainable, this trader may not be in the allowed trader class. So mere computability by a stronger (A) is not enough in the original time scale.

That means the sentence:

> “A computes the quote, so (Q_A) is computable, so closure under conditioning applies”

is too fast.

## The online/process framing that does work

The fix is to make the conditioning stream consist of **public emitted quote facts**, indexed by the time at which they are actually emitted.

Define an e.c. quote process (D'_A) as follows:

At each global day (t), the coupled system simulates whatever computation (A) is allowed to perform up to that day. If (A) has emitted a rounded quote profile by day (t), (D'_A) includes the corresponding finite quote sentence. If not, (D'_A) adds nothing new, or only a harmless tautology.

Then (D'_A) is e.c. in the global time parameter: to compute its contents up to day (t), simulate the public quote-emission procedure up to day (t). The quote may be hard for (H)-level traders to predict **before it is emitted**, but once emitted it is just a public sentence in (D'_A).

Then define

[
H^+*t = H_t(-\mid Q*{A,<t}),
]

where (Q_{A,<t}) is the conjunction of quote facts emitted before day (t). This exactly matches the G.8 proof pattern: (D'_A) is the extra e.c. process; (\psi^\circ_t) is the conjunction of quote facts emitted so far; (H^+) is the conditional market.

So the online formulation works if we time-index quotes by **emission time**, not by an abstract advice index (n) whose quote might require superpolynomial computation in (n).

## Does this collapse the complexity gap?

No. It only says the emitted quote stream is public and effectively enumerable once produced.

The distinction is:

[
\text{H can enumerate already-emitted quote facts}
]

versus

[
\text{H can predict future quote facts before A emits them}.
]

Closure under conditioning needs the first. The model’s epistemic authority story requires the second to fail.

So it is perfectly coherent to say:

* (A) is in a stronger computational class.
* (H)-level traders cannot efficiently predict (A)’s future quotes.
* Once (A) emits a quote, that quote becomes part of an e.c. public condition stream.
* (H^+) is (H) conditioned on the public quote stream so far.

That is exactly the setup we want.

## The time-dilation cost

There is a cost: if (A)’s computation takes a long time, the quote only appears when it appears. You cannot say “on day (n), condition on (A)’s (n)-th superhard quote” unless the quote is efficiently computable by day (n).

Instead, say:

> On day (t), (H^+) conditions on all quote facts emitted by (A) before day (t).

Then a quote about (P^{(n)}) may be emitted at some later public time (e(n)). The deferral function (F(n)) and settlement time (\sigma(n)) should be stated relative to the **emission time**:

[
e(n) < F(n) < \sigma(n).
]

That keeps the recursion well-founded and keeps the condition stream e.c.

## How this fits the G.8 proof

The G.8 proof first fixes a base deductive process (D) and another e.c. process (D'), then considers conditioning on the conjunction of all sentences that have appeared in (D') up to time (n). It proves the conditional market is a logical inductor over the combined process (D_n\cup D'_n). 

In our setting:

* (D) is the base human deductive process.
* (D'_A) is the public quote-emission process.
* (\psi^\circ_t) is the conjunction of quote facts emitted so far.
* (H^+_t) is (H_t(-\mid \psi^\circ_t)).

The proof’s trader construction needs (D'_A) to be e.c. because it builds trades involving (\psi^\circ_t). It does **not** require (H) to know future quote facts. It only requires the cumulative condition at time (t) to be effectively available in the formal time parameter.

## Bottom line

The online framing works if stated this way:

> Although (A)’s future quotes need not be efficiently predictable by (H), the realized quote stream is emitted as a public e.c. process. (H^+_t) conditions only on quote facts emitted before time (t). Thus the quote facts form the auxiliary e.c. deductive process (D'_A) required by the proof of Closure Under Conditioning. The complexity gap is preserved because (H) need not compute future quotes; it only conditions on already-published ones.

What does **not** work is conditioning on a non-e.c. sequence of ideal quote facts indexed by the original query number. We need the public online emission schedule.

Two different questions hide in there, and separating them is the whole ballgame. The first is about legitimacy of the *bookkeeping*; the second is about whether the *object is worth building*. The bookkeeping is fine. The second is where I think the construction is in real trouble — and your instinct is pointing right at it.

**Can the simulation be done, even slowly?** Yes, but notice *who* does it. It isn't H simulating A. It's a *trader* — an external e.c. program — running the joint (A, H⁺) system forward for t elementary steps, which is O(t) by the triviality that a TM's t-step output is poly(t)-computable. The trader never predicts or outruns anything; it turns the crank t times and reads off whatever profiles got emitted. Well-foundedness (F(i) < σ(i), the quote for i settles after H⁺ has passed F(i)) means each step needs only earlier data, so there's no vicious loop. So "e.c. in emission time" is legit. But that legitimacy is exactly what should make you suspicious, because it means A's emitted quotes *are* computable by an e.c.-in-t program — the only thing that's hard is that the quote about P^(n) doesn't appear until step e(n), which is exponential in n. The complexity gap, honestly stated, is just: A's quote about P^(n) costs ~e(n) ≈ EXP(n) elementary steps to have in hand, and an H-level (poly-in-n) reasoner can't have it "at stage n." Fine so far.

**Now the real question, and here's the trap.** How does A come to know Y_n = H⁺_{F(n)}? There are two stories and they have opposite consequences.

If A knows Y_n by *simulating* H⁺ out to stage F(n), then emitting the quote costs ~c(F(n)) elementary steps — and c(F(n)) is *also exactly the step at which H⁺, running normally, reaches stage F(n) and has Y_n itself*. So e(n) ≳ c(F(n)): A's quote lands no earlier than H⁺'s own answer. In that story the construction is legit and completely useless — A is an oracle that finishes computing your future at the same moment your future arrives. No acceleration, period. This is the worst case, and nothing in the machinery rules it out.

The escape — and the only thing that makes the paper non-empty — is that A is **not** a simulator. A is a logical inductor; its quote a_n is a *prediction* made by its market from patterns in *already-settled* contracts (i with σ(i) < e(n)), not a simulation of H⁺ to F(n). Tracking (a_n − Y_n → 0) is precisely the statement that these predictions are calibrated in the limit — A guesses Y_n before it could ever simulate it. So the useful version of the story is: A, with 𝓒_A power, extracts structure from H⁺'s settled track record that H⁺ (𝓒_H) cannot extract about itself, and generalizes to not-yet-resolved sentences *cheaply* — far cheaper than c(F(n)). When that happens, e(n) ≪ c(F(n)) and H⁺ genuinely jumps to a good estimate of its own deferred belief early. That is real usefulness, and it's the thing the complexity gap is *supposed* to buy: better generalization, not faster simulation.

**But here's what the current theorems do and don't give you.** Tracking establishes *calibration*. It says nothing about *rate*. Logical induction has no rate guarantees anywhere — every property is "eventually," with no handle on when. So "A's quote about P^(n) is good *before* F(n)" is not a consequence of Tracking; it's an extra, un-established, and frankly un-guaranteeable-in-general property. The framework permits A to be calibrated only "very late," in which case H⁺ gains nothing operationally before its deferral target. So the honest status is: the construction guarantees an asymptotically-calibrated external predictor of H⁺'s own deferred futures (non-vacuous — arbitrary data wouldn't track), but it does **not** guarantee acceleration, and the "arrive faster at humanity's trusted beliefs" motivation is, as written, not a theorem and possibly not true without further assumptions. (~80% on that being the correct read; the rate-free nature of LI is ~90%.)

So to answer you directly: it's legit, and it's useful *only in the cases where A's advantage shows up as cheap generalization rather than expensive simulation* — and the present theorems can't tell those cases apart, because calibration is blind to rate. The "is it ever useful" worry is not paranoia; it's the load-bearing gap.

Two ways forward, and I'd push you toward the second unless you're feeling ambitious. (a) Make acceleration a real theorem: impose structure on {Y_n} (e.g. the deferred futures lie in some 𝓒_A-learnable-but-not-𝓒_H-learnable class) and prove an *earliness/rate* result — that A's quote is ε-good by some e(n) provably below F(n). That's hard, it's a genuinely new result, and it's arguably the actual research contribution lurking here. (b) Drop "faster" from the thesis and reframe the contribution as trust *relocation*: External Trust says H⁺ can move its self-trust off an uncomputable future credence and onto A's concrete, inspectable, present quote — a calibrated external proxy you can *look at and check*, which is your kernel/context point exactly. That story the theorems actually support, and it doesn't depend on any rate. The speed claim is the part that's writing a check the logical-induction account can't cash.

The thing I'd stop doing is letting "A is more computationally powerful" silently stand in for "A is faster for H's purposes." Those come apart precisely here: A's power is real, but unless it manifests as generalization that beats simulation, it buys calibration without buying time — and calibration-without-time is inspectability, not acceleration.

\title{Trust Between Universal Inductors}

\begin{sloppypar}

\subsection*{Motivation}

Let $H$ be a universal inductor, in the sense of a \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.03543}{logical inductor} conditioned on bitstrings that represent the proven theorems of a deductive process.\footnote{Here we're primarily using
\href{https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/FnH2G832sWMySptp5}{this explanation of universal inductors} by ``Diffractor'' as a guide for the setup.} $H$ should be thought of as a bounded reasoner that, in some way, represents evolving human opinions over time. Then, suppose another universal inductor $A$ is constructed as a strictly more computationally powerful reasoner that is trying to predict the future states of the human reasoner (with good feedback about what those future states turn out to be.) Suppose then that we condition $H$ further on bitstrings representing outputs of $A$, in an attempt to leverage an AI's additional computational power to arrive faster at humanity's own trusted future beliefs. The following construction makes this setup concrete. [Summary of findings after finishing]


\subsection*{Construction}

\paragraph{Base reasoner.}
Take a propositional language $\mathcal{L}$ with sentence set $\mathcal{S}$, a
theory $\Gamma$, and a $\Gamma$-complete computable deductive process
$D_H=(D_H^t)_{t\ge1}$. Let $\mathcal{C}_H$ be a complexity class closed under
polynomial overhead \footnote{explanation of polynomial overhead} and let $H=(H_1,H_2,\ldots)$ be a \emph{universal inductor}
over $D_H$ against $\mathcal{C}_H$: a market each of whose stages $H_t$ is a probability measure over the worlds of $\mathcal{L}$, concentrated on
the worlds propositionally consistent with $D_H^t$, satisfying the logical induction
criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$. Existence of such a
measure-valued inductor over an arbitrary computable deductive process is
Lemma~\ref{lem:existence}.

\paragraph{Propositions and deferral.}
Choose a strictly increasing, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable ``deferral" function
$F:\mathbb{N}^+\to\mathbb{N}^+$ with $F(n)>n+1$. Fix an effective enumeration
$P^{(0)},P^{(1)},\ldots$ of $\mathcal{S}$. Since the enumeration is arbitrary, take
$P^{(n)}$ to be some $n$-th proposition of interest, so that tying contract $n$
to statement $P^{(n)}$ costs no generality.

\paragraph{Threshold symbols.}
For each $n\ge1$ and $1\le k\le n$ introduce two fresh propositional symbols:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $\alpha_{n,k}$ representing ``the contract for $P^{(n)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $k/n$";
  \item $\beta_{n,k}$ representing ``$A$'s published quote for that contract is at least $k/n$."
\end{itemize}
Let $\mathcal{L}^\alpha:=\mathcal{L}\cup\{\alpha_{n,k}\}$ and
$\mathcal{L}^\beta:=\mathcal{L}\cup\{\beta_{n,k}\}$, with sentence sets
$\mathcal{S}^\alpha$ and $\mathcal{S}^\beta$ respectively, each extending $\mathcal{S}$. The $\alpha$ symbols allow $A$ to price
the future credences of $H^+$ while the $\beta$ symbols
encode $A$'s outputs for $H^+$ to condition on. Because each of these sets of symbols represents threshold sentences, that is claims that a value is at least $\frac{k}{n}$, they respect the monotonicity axioms:
\[
\{\alpha_{n,k}\to\alpha_{n,k-1}\}\quad\text{and}\quad
\{\beta_{n,k}\to\beta_{n,k-1}\}\qquad(n\ge1,\ 2\le k\le n).
\]
For a world $W$ consistent with these axioms each truth-set is an initial
segment, so we can define values as proportions of true threshold sentences:
\[
\mathrm{val}^\alpha_W(n):=\tfrac1n\#\{k:W(\alpha_{n,k})=1\},
\qquad
\mathrm{val}^\beta_W(n):=\tfrac1n\#\{k:W(\beta_{n,k})=1\}
\]
each taking the form $m/n$ for an integer $0\le m\le n$. Using these values, the addition of the threshold symbols to the language allows for the representation of a real-valued unknown rounded to the nearest $\frac{1}{n}$.

\paragraph{Contracts and quotes.}
Define the deferred contract $C_n$ and the quote readout $Q_n$ as affine combinations
\[
C_n:=\tfrac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\alpha_{n,k},
\qquad
Q_n:=\tfrac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\beta_{n,k},
\]
so $W(C_n)=\mathrm{val}^\alpha_W(n)$ and $W(Q_n)=\mathrm{val}^\beta_W(n)$
for consistent worlds $W$. Note that both $C_n$ and $Q_n$ are affine combinations of symbols
already in the markets used for convenience rather than separately traded objects. Write
\[
a_n:=A_n(C_n)=\tfrac1n\sum_k A_n(\alpha_{n,k})\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]
\]
for $A$'s published quote on the deferred contract and
\[
Y_n:=H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})
\]
for the eventual credence of $H^+$ that the contract uses for settlement. 

\paragraph{A more powerful reasoner.}
Let $\mathcal{C}_A\supseteq\mathcal{C}_H$ be a complexity class closed under
polynomial overhead for which the map $n\mapsto Y_n$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
in the coupled system. More precisely, given $n$, an implementation in $\mathcal{C}_A$ can simulate the mutual construction up to stage $F(n)$ and output $Y_n$. Writing $R(t)$ for the per-stage runtime of the
implementation of $H^+$, we assume $\mathcal{C}_A$ contains $n\mapsto R(F(n))$ (e.g.\ $\mathcal{C}_H=\mathrm{P}$, $\mathcal{C}_A=\mathrm{EXP}$, $F(n)=2^n$ when
$R$ is polynomial). This is a significant idealizing assumption about the computational power of $A$ needed so that its deferred bets can eventually deductively resolve, but note that the simulation need not be practically implementable by the traders. Let $\sigma:\mathbb{N}^+\to\mathbb{N}^+$ be
$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable with $\sigma(n)>F(n)$ and such that $Y_n$ can be computed by this simulation
within $\sigma(n)$ steps, meaning that markets for $C_n$ resolve by time $\sigma(n)$.

\paragraph{The inductor $A$.}
We will now define $A$ and $H^+$ as two inductors that can see each other, constructed via recursion. For $0\le m\le n$ write the settling profile 
\[
\mathcal{A}_n(m):=\{\alpha_{n,k}:k\le m\}\cup\{\neg\alpha_{n,k}:k>m\}
\]
which should be read as ``$C_n$ is approximately equal to $\frac{m}{n}$. Let
\[
m_n^*:=\argmin_{0\le m\le n}\left|\tfrac mn-Y_n\right|
\]
with ties going to the lower $m$, i.e. the best approximation of the real-valued settlement $Y_n$. We therefore have
\[
\left|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n}-Y_n\right|\le\tfrac1{2n}
\]
because the grid $\{0,\frac1n,\frac2n,\ldots,1\}$ has spacing $\frac1n$, so every value in $[0,1]$ is within $\frac1{2n}$ of some grid point. Define the computable deductive process
$D_A$ over $\mathcal{L}^\alpha$ as one that, for each time step $t$, $D_A^t$ includes the $\alpha$-monotonicity axioms for $n\le t$ and the profile $\mathcal{A}_n(m_n^*)$ for each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\le t$.
Each $D_A^t$ is finite (axiom schemata and settlement profiles are finite at any finite stage) and consistent (distinct $n$ touch disjoint symbols for both axioms and profiles, settlements are initial segments respecting monotonicity). $D_A$ is
computable as part of the mutual construction, since $\sigma(n)>F(n)$ makes $Y_n$ available from $H^+$
before its settlement is required by $D_A$. Let $A=(A_1,A_2,\ldots)$ be a universal
inductor over $D_A$ against $\mathcal{C}_A$.

\paragraph{The inductor $H^+$.}
Symmetrically write
\[
\mathcal{B}_n(\ell):=\{\beta_{n,k}:k\le\ell\}\cup\{\neg\beta_{n,k}:k>\ell\}
\]
for a profile associated with a posted quote and let
\[
\ell_n^*:=\argmin_{0\le\ell\le n}\left|\tfrac\ell n-a_n\right|
\]
with ties going to the lower $\ell$. This is the rounding of $A$'s quote to a grid with spacing $\frac{1}{n}$ . Take the base inductor $H$ to be defined over the extended language $\mathcal{L}^\beta$, with the $\beta$-monotonicity axioms adjoined to $\Gamma$, so that it assigns credences to $A$'s quote atoms. Writing
\[
Q_A^{(t)}:=\bigwedge_{i<t}\mathcal{B}_i(\ell_i^*)
\]
for the one-step-delayed record of $A$'s published quotes available by time $t$, define the augmented human inductor by conditioning,
\[
H^+:=H\mid Q_A,\qquad H^+_t(\cdot):=H_t\!\left(\,\cdot\mid Q_A^{(t)}\right).
\]
By closure under conditioning (Garrabrant et al., Theorem 4.7.2), $H^+$ is again a universal inductor against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$, now over $\Gamma$ together with the asserted quote profiles. The conditioning event $Q_A^{(t)}$ is finite and propositionally consistent, and it is computable as part of the recursion since all of the quotes it records are available by time $t$.

\subsection*{Results}
\paragraph{Existence and well-foundedness.}
The four sequences $(A_t),(H^+_t),(D_A^t),(Q_A^{(t)})$ are defined by one
recursion on $t$. $D_A^t$ depends on $H^+$ through values of $H^+_{F(i)}$ for $i$ with $\sigma(i)\le t$, hence $F(i)<\sigma(i)\le t$: prices
at times strictly below $t$. The conditioning event $Q_A^{(t)}$ depends on $A$ only through quotes $a_i$
for $i<t$, again strictly below $t$. Neither market's stage-$t$ pricing
references the other's stage-$t$ pricing, so every stage-$t$ object is determined
by data from some stage less than $t$. Lemma 1 carries out the recursion and
verifies the two markets satisfy their logical induction criteria.

\begin{lemma}[Existence]\label{lem:existence} Assume the computational idealization in the construction: the map
\[
n\mapsto Y_n:=H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})
\]
is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable in the mutually defined system, and
$\sigma(n)>F(n)$ is a $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable schedule by which $Y_n$ can be
computed. Then the recursive construction of
\[
(A_t),\quad (H^+_t),\quad (D_A^t),\quad (Q_A^{(t)})
\]
is well-founded. Moreover, each $D_A^t$ is finite and
propositionally consistent, each conditioning event $Q_A^{(t)}$ is consistent with
$\Gamma$, $A$ is a logical inductor over $D_A$ against
$\mathcal{C}_A$, and $H^+=H\mid Q_A$ is a logical inductor against
$\mathcal{C}_H$ by closure under conditioning (Garrabrant et al., Theorem 4.7.2).
\end{lemma}
\paragraph{Limit calibration of $A$ tracking $H^+$.} Placeholder intro
\begin{theorem}[Tracking] In the coupled system above,\[
a_n-Y_n\to 0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
A_n(C_n)-H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\to 0.
\] 
\end{theorem}
\paragraph{A reflection principle for $H^+$ about $A$.} We next turn to a form of reflection-style \footnote{In the sense of van Fraassen's reflection principle} trust created by this coupled system. The following theorem is a close variation of Garrabrant's Theorem 4.12.4 on Self-Trust in which $H^+$ conditions not on its own future credence directly, but on a quote from $A$ encoded in the $\beta$ atoms.

For a rational tolerance $\delta>0$ and a real-valued expression $X\in[0,1]$, define the one-sided continuous indicator
\[
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(X>p) :=
\begin{cases}
0 & X\le p,\\[2pt]
\dfrac{X-p}{\delta} & p<X<p+\delta,\\[4pt]
1 & X\ge p+\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
Define $\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(X<p)$ analogously, i.e. with value 0 for $X$ at least $p$, value 1 for $X$ more than $\delta$ less than $p$, and linearly interpolated between 0 and 1 for $X$ at most $\delta$ less than $p$.

Recall that the quote readout (i.e. the price for the contract $C_n$ rounded to the $\frac{1}{n}$ grid) is defined as \[Q_n:=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\beta_{n,k}\]

We use the standard extension of logical induction from sentence-prices to expectations of bounded finite logically uncertain variables (LUVs).\footnote{Definition 4.8.1 of Garrabrant et al.} In particular, any bounded rational-valued function of finitely many sentences can be expanded as a finite affine combination of conjunctions over their truth profiles, priced by linearity. The variables appearing below, such as $1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)$, depend only on the finite family of atoms $\{\beta_{n,k}:1\le k\le n\}$ together with the sentence $P^{(n)}$, and so are legitimate bounded finite LUVs.

\begin{theorem}[External trust]\label{thm:external-trust}
Let $(p_n)$ be a $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable sequence of rational probabilities in
$[0,1]$, and let $\delta>0$ be rational. Write $1(P^{(n)})$ for the $[0,1]$-LUV representing the truth value of $P^{(n)}$. Then
\[
H^+_n\!\left(
1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)
\right)
\gtrsim_n
p_n\,
H^+_n\!\left(
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)
\right).
\]
Similarly,
\[
H^+_n\!\left(
1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n<p_n)
\right)
\lesssim_n
p_n\,
H^+_n\!\left(
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n<p_n)
\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

No, it's not an issue, and here's the clean way to see why the gap and the e.c. requirement never actually collide.

The e.c. condition 4.7.2 wants is a property *per stage of H's clock*: the conditioning set $D_A'^{\,n}$ must be computable in poly(n). The complexity gap is a property *per contract index*: computing a single quote $a_m$ costs $T_A(m)$, A's runtime, which is super-polynomial in m. These are measured against different parameters, and the emission schedule is exactly the device that keeps the second from contaminating the first.

The cleanest statement of why: define $D_A'^{\,n}$ as "the profiles the simulation has emitted after n steps." Then it is *tautologically* poly(n)-computable — it's the output of n steps of a fixed machine, which you produce by running n steps. There's no way for that to be expensive in n; it's O(n) by definition. So whatever A's complexity is, "the quotes published by stage n" is always e.c. in n.

Where does the gap go, then? Into *latency*. Computing $a_m$ takes $T_A(m)$ steps, so the simulation can't emit contract m's quote until stage $e(m) \approx T_A(m)$ — exponentially far out if A is exponential, doubly-exponentially far if A is doubly-exponential. So at stage n the only quotes present are those for $m \le e^{-1}(n)$, and each of those, by construction, cost $\le n$ steps to produce, hence $\le$ poly(n) to recompute. The bigger the gap between A and H, the *later* each quote sits on H's clock — never the more expensive it is to read off the record once it's there. The gap is converted into how far out the useful quotes live, not into per-stage cost.

The conceptual frame that dissolves the apparent tension is prediction versus consumption:

- "A is in a higher class" means precisely that H-level computation cannot *predict* $a_m$ — cannot compute it as a function of the contract index m within a poly(m) budget. That's $T_A(m)$ being super-poly, and it's intact; it's the whole reason A is worth deferring to.
- "the emitted sequence is e.c." means H-level computation can *consume* the stream — recompute what's already on the public record by stage n within poly(n). That's cheap because publication is scheduled to never outrun consumability.

There's no contradiction between "can't predict the next quote" and "can read the quotes already posted," and 4.7.2 only needs the second. That's also exactly the asymmetry you want for the epistemic-authority story: H⁺'s traders cannot anticipate A (gap preserved) but can verify A's published outputs (stream e.c.), which is what makes the trust both non-trivial and grounded.

The one real obligation this puts on the construction — state it explicitly rather than hide it — is that the schedule must dominate A's runtime, $e(m) \gtrsim T_A(m)$, which is automatic if you simply define emission as "publish $a_m$ when the simulation finishes computing it." \begin{itemize}

\{\beta_{n,k}\to\beta_{n,k-1}\}\qquad(n\ge1,\ 2\le k\le n).

by data from some stage less than $t$. Lemma 1 carries out the recursion and
verifies the two markets satisfy their logical induction criteria.

is well-founded. Moreover, each $D_A^t$ is finite and

We use the standard extension of logical induction from sentence-prices to expectations of bounded finite logically uncertain variables (LUVs).\footnote{Definition 4.8.1 of Garrabrant et al.} In particular, any bounded rational-valued function of finitely many sentences can be expanded as a finite affine combination of conjunctions over their truth profiles, priced by linearity. Let $(p_n)$ be a $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable sequence of rational probabilities in

\[

1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)
\right)
\gtrsim_n
p_n\,
H^+_n\!\left(
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)
\right).
\]
Similarly,
\[
H^+_n\!\left(
1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n<p_n)
\right)
\lesssim_n
p_n\,
H^+_n\!\left(
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n<p_n)
\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

Good instinct to red-team it now. Here's where I'd attack it, roughly in order of how much damage a good referee can do. You've got the usefulness one; I'll sharpen it and add the ones I think are more dangerous than you may be weighting.

**1. Genre confusion: is this a proposal or a warning?** This is the one that does the most damage, and it's upstream of your "get there faster" point. The motivation reads as a *proposal* — "leverage an AI to arrive faster at humanity's trusted beliefs." But the actual content, once the pull section lands, is closer to an *impossibility-flavored characterization*: deference to a stronger predictor creates a belief-shifting channel that is useful on verifiable claims and uncorrectably manipulable on unverifiable ones, recursively inseparably. If you present a proposal and then prove it doesn't deliver the benefit cleanly and does deliver a harm, a referee kills it on its own terms. If you present it as "here is the structure of the usefulness/manipulability tradeoff in AI deference, and here is why no computable policy separates the horns," it's a contribution. Same theorems, opposite reception. Pick the second genre explicitly and the "arrive faster" sentence stops being a liability and becomes the setup for the tradeoff. So I think your "make the usefulness claim honest" instinct is right but undersells the fix — it's not hedging a sentence, it's changing what the paper claims to be.

**2. A is rewarded for predicting H⁺'s *opinions*, not the truth — and the self-reference buys exactly the bad part.** This is the deepest setup objection and the one I'd expect from Demski or anyone in the debate/ELK orbit. Your contracts settle against $Y_n = H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})$ — H⁺'s own future *credence* — not against $P^{(n)}$'s truth. You have to do this (no feedback on never-resolving sentences), but the consequence is that a perfectly accurate A is one that predicts what H⁺ will come to believe, including its mistakes, and on Φ that's a closed loop with no contact with anything external. The sharp version: *the self-referential coupling is unnecessary for the good case and constitutive of the bad one.* On R, you don't need A to settle against H⁺'s future credence — A could just predict the resolution, and H⁺ defers to a better forecaster of facts. The H⁺-predicts-A-predicts-H⁺ fixed point only adds content on Φ, where that content is manipulation. A skeptic will say you've engineered precisely the structure that generates the pathology and called it the feature. You need a principled answer to "why settle against future credence rather than eventual truth," and the honest one is value-laden: for the claims we actually care about (normative ones) there *is* no eventual resolution, so idealized future credence is the best target available. But that answer commits you to the next objection.

**3. The metaethics tension — and it's also an opportunity.** Settling against idealized future credence is a *constructivist/anti-realist* move: the target is "what H would come to believe," not a mind-independent fact. You're a non-naturalist realist. A referee who knows your commitments (or just reads carefully) will say the formal setup encodes the metaethics you reject — and worse, that on the realist view the danger isn't only manipulation: even a perfectly faithful, non-manipulative A drives H⁺ to its idealized credence, which a realist must allow could be *wrong* (idealized credence ≠ moral fact). The constructive flip, which I'd actually put in the paper: your Murdochian line is that conscience is a fallible-but-reliable perceptual faculty. Reliabilism about conscience says idealized credence-under-good-conditions tracks the fact — which is exactly the R-fragment (credence → something it's answerable to) — and *fails* to track on the cases with no answerability, which is Φ. So your metaethics predicts the R/Φ split rather than conflicting with it. If you draw that line explicitly you convert a vulnerability into a motivation for why the resolving/non-resolving boundary is the morally load-bearing one. Leave it latent and a critic uses it against you.

**4. The theorems may read as corollaries, and one step isn't proved.** Tracking is "calibration from feedback (4.3.8) applied to contracts that settle against $Y_n$" — a referee will call it immediate unless you foreground what's non-trivial (the coupling makes it a fixed point; it holds uniformly across the complexity gap). External Trust is "4.12.4 plus a Lipschitz swap." More pressingly, the swap is not actually proved: it needs $H^+_n(|Q_n - Y_n|)\to 0$ — H⁺ must *believe* the readout tracks its future credence — and right now that's asserted via Tracking, but Tracking is about the realized values, not about H⁺'s priced belief. Getting from "the values converge" to "H⁺ prices them as converging" is a real step (it's the learned-generalization point), and a careful referee will demand it. That's the most concrete proof gap in the current draft.

**5. The idealization is enormous and possibly non-embedded — Demski's likely angle.** "A can simulate the entire coupled system up to $F(n)$" is A out-computing a system it is part of. You've handled well-foundedness, but a referee focused on embedded agency will ask whether the idealization is consistent and non-vacuous: does an admissible tuple $(\mathcal C_H,\mathcal C_A,F,\sigma,e,\text{coupled system})$ provably exist, and is the existence non-trivial (not "assume what you need")? Right now it's gestured at with P/EXP; I'd want a clean existence paragraph, because "$A$ simulates everything including the H⁺ that conditions on $A$" is exactly where a skeptic looks for hidden circularity even after well-foundedness is established.

**6. Results are possibility-level, not necessity.** We established the trust/manipulation on Φ is *selection*, not forced (no arbitrage on never-resolving sentences). So both the positive ("H⁺ benefits") and negative ("A manipulates") are "there exists an admissible coupling where…", not "every admissible coupling." A referee will note the paper proves *possibility* on Φ and want to know what's generic. You can't make it forced (we checked — the mechanism is absent), so you have to state the possibility-level honestly and not let prose drift into "H⁺ *will* be manipulated."

**7. The emission apparatus is itself an attack surface — your confidence about the conditioning may be a touch high.** The conditioning is now *defensible*, yes. But the emission clock is baroque, and a referee's natural question is "why pay for it?" — i.e. why not define H⁺ by ordinary existence over $\Gamma\cup\{\text{profiles}\}$ (route b) and drop the e.c. bookkeeping entirely? The only answer is "to keep H⁺ literally $H$'s conditional so the non-conservativity comparison is one reasoner against itself," and given that the token's behavior on Φ is selection-dependent anyway, a referee may judge the apparatus not worth the determinacy. I wouldn't call the conditioning a weak point exactly, but "is the machinery earning the determinate token" is a live question a referee will raise, and I'd have the one-paragraph defense ready rather than treat it as settled.

**8. Positioning.** "AI predicts the human's idealized future endorsement and the human defers" is adjacent to recursive reward modeling, amplification, debate, ELK, and indirect-normativity/CEV. The manipulation-indistinguishable-from-help result rhymes with known reward-hacking and auditing-game results. The genuinely new thing is the logical-induction formalization and the *recursive-inseparability* characterization of the tradeoff — that's a real contribution, but if you don't situate it a referee reads it as reformalizing folklore.

On your two stated points: usefulness — yes, and the key is that it can't be a separate positive bolt-on. State it so its hypothesis (a class separation on a resolving-within-horizon family) is the *same object* that, by R/Φ inseparability, drags in the Φ-exposure. Then "useful" and "manipulable" aren't two results, they're one theorem with two consequences you can't decouple — which is both the honest claim and the interesting one. On Bayesian conditioning — it's justifiable, but per #7 the live question isn't "is it well-defined" (you've earned that) but "is the token worth the apparatus," and that's where the pushback will actually come from.

If I had to name the single thing most likely to sink it with a strong referee: #1 and #2 together — the paper currently markets a benefit it characterizes away, using a self-referential mechanism whose only distinctive content is the harm. Fix the genre and give the principled "why future credence" answer (#3), and most of the rest is normal revision.

Pulled the actual Diffractor posts, and they answer this cleanly — your option 4 is essentially right, and options 1–3 are facets of the same picture rather than alternatives.

The definition: a universal inductor is a distribution over infinite bitstrings whose prefix probabilities are computable, where the nth atomic statement is "the nth bit is a 1," and the sequence of probability assignments forms a logical inductor over the empty deductive process. So your option 1 is literally the definition of the *base* object — it's a logical inductor over the empty theory, living on the language of bit-atoms, equivalently a computable measure over all infinite bitstrings (all worlds).

The "universal" part is exactly your option 4. Because it's a distribution over bitstrings, you can make it act as a logical inductor over any theory you like — PA, ZFC, second-order arithmetic — by fixing an efficiently computable map from bits to sentences, conditioning the universal inductor on the bits corresponding to proven theorems, and reading off the probabilities of other bits from the resulting conditional. The same universal inductor yields a logical inductor over PA by looking at some conditionals and over ZFC by looking at others — which is where the name comes from. So options 2 and 3 are the *derived* objects: a "regular" logical inductor over a deductive process D just *is* the universal inductor conditioned on D's theorem-bits. They're the same kind of thing; the universal one is the un-conditioned master, and conditioning on different bits (deductive-process bits, or any other data) gives you the specific inductors.

And the mechanism is precisely the one we've been wrangling: the trick works by Theorem 4.7.2, Closure Under Conditioning — conditioning a logical inductor on a sequence of non-inconsistent sentences yields a logical inductor over the deductive process where those conditionals hold. So every "conditioning" in your paper, including the one that produces H itself, is 4.7.2 on the universal inductor. That's why the e.c. requirement we spent so long on isn't a special burden you took on by conditioning on A — it's the *same* condition that's silently satisfied when you condition on a deductive process (a deductive process is automatically an e.c. bit-sequence), and the only reason A's quotes needed the emission schedule is that they're the one bit-stream that isn't automatically e.c. in the contract index.

Two things worth pulling out, because they bear on your framing decisions.

First, the load-bearing reason to say "universal" rather than just "logical inductor." A universal inductor corresponds to a logical inductor, but the associated one does not have finite support, so it differs from the LIA constructed in the paper. That non-finite-support, full-measure-over-worlds character is exactly what makes conditioning well-behaved — you can condition a full measure on an event, whereas Garrabrant's finite-support LIA isn't a clean object to Bayes-condition. This is the pivot you already made (LIA → universal inductors for genuine conditioning), and now you can see it's not a stylistic choice: the universal-inductor formalism is *the* thing that licenses the conditioning your whole construction runs on. So when a referee asks "is the universal-inductor framing decorative?" the answer is no — drop it and you lose the right to condition.

Second, this actually sharpens the route-(a)-vs-(b) question and tilts it toward conditioning. In this framing, H = U ∣ (D_H bits) for some base universal inductor U, and H⁺ = H ∣ (A bits) = U ∣ (D_H ∧ A bits), since conditioning is associative. That's a *canonical* object once you've fixed U — it's not "some logical inductor over Γ ∪ {profiles}," it's specifically the universal inductor restricted to the combined data. So the determinate token you wanted isn't fixed by an arbitrary existence choice; it's fixed by the base universal inductor, and "condition H further on A" is the same operation that built H. Route (b) — a fresh inductor over the augmented process — corresponds to picking a *different* base, which is exactly what breaks the "same H" relationship. So the universal-inductor framing is what makes route (a) the natural one, and it's the cleanest answer to the "why not just build it fresh" pushback.

The one caveat to keep honest: "the same operation, just different bits" is true for *well-definedness*, but the bits are not epistemically on a par. Conditioning on D_H's theorem-bits is conditioning on logical facts; conditioning on A's quote-bits is conditioning on a strategic agent's outputs. The formalism flattens them into "more bits to condition on," and that flattening is precisely what lets A's freely-chosen quotes ride in through the same channel as proven theorems — which is the manipulation story. So the elegance of "it's all just conditioning the universal inductor" is real and worth using in the setup, but it's also exactly the move a critic will point at when they ask why A's outputs get to enter H's beliefs by the same mechanism as PA's theorems.

\subsection*{Motivation}

Let $H$ be a \emph{universal inductor}, in the sense of a \href{https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.03543}{logical inductor} conditioned on consistent infinite bitstrings. \footnote{The basic construction is given in
\href{https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/FnH2G832sWMySptp5}{this explanation of universal inductors} by Diffractor.} $H$ should be thought of as a bounded reasoner that represents evolving human opinions over time, constructed by conditioning on bitstring representations of empirical observations and proven theorems. We then construct a new inductor $H^+$ by conditioning $H$ further on bitstrings representing outputs of $A$. This may be thought of as an attempt to leverage an AI's additional computational power to gain information about humanity's own trusted future beliefs. The following construction makes this setup concrete. [Summary of findings after finishing]


\subsection*{Construction}

\paragraph{Base reasoner.}
Take a propositional language $\mathcal{L}$ with sentence set $\mathcal{S}$, a
theory $\Gamma$, and a $\Gamma$-complete computable deductive process

over $D_H$ against $\mathcal{C}_H$: a market each of whose stages $H_t$ is a probability measure over the worlds of $\mathcal{L}$, concentrated on
the worlds propositionally consistent with $D_H^t$, satisfying the logical induction
criterion against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$. Existence of such a
measure-valued inductor over an arbitrary computable deductive process is
Lemma~\ref{lem:existence}.

\paragraph{Propositions and deferral.}
Choose a strictly increasing, $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable ``deferral" function
$F:\mathbb{N}^+\to\mathbb{N}^+$ with $F(n)>n+1$. Fix an effective enumeration
$P^{(0)},P^{(1)},\ldots$ of $\mathcal{S}$. Since the enumeration is arbitrary, take
$P^{(n)}$ to be some $n$-th proposition of interest, so that tying contract $n$
to statement $P^{(n)}$ costs no generality.

\paragraph{Threshold symbols.}
For each $n\ge1$ and $1\le k\le n$ introduce two fresh propositional symbols:
\begin{itemize}
  \item $\alpha_{n,k}$ representing ``the contract for $P^{(n)}$ deferred to $F(n)$ has value at least $k/n$";
  \item $\beta_{n,k}$ representing ``$A$'s published quote for that contract is at least $k/n$."

\{\beta_{n,k}\to\beta_{n,k-1}\}\qquad(n\ge1,\ 2\le k\le n).
\]

\mathrm{val}^\beta_W(n):=\tfrac1n\#\{k:W(\beta_{n,k})=1\}

each taking the form $m/n$ for an integer $0\le m\le n$. Using these values, the addition of the threshold symbols to the language allows for the representation of a real-valued unknown rounded to the nearest $\frac{1}{n}$.

\paragraph{Contracts and quotes.}
Define the deferred contract $C_n$ and the quote readout $Q_n$ as affine combinations
\[
C_n:=\tfrac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\alpha_{n,k},
\qquad
Q_n:=\tfrac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\beta_{n,k},
\]
so $W(C_n)=\mathrm{val}^\alpha_W(n)$ and $W(Q_n)=\mathrm{val}^\beta_W(n)$
for consistent worlds $W$. Note that both $C_n$ and $Q_n$ are affine combinations of symbols
already in the markets used for convenience rather than separately traded objects. Write
\[
a_n:=A_n(C_n)=\tfrac1n\sum_k A_n(\alpha_{n,k})\in\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]
\]
for $A$'s published quote on the deferred contract and
\[

\]
for the eventual credence of $H^+$ that the contract uses for settlement. 

\paragraph{A more powerful reasoner.}
Let $\mathcal{C}_A\supseteq\mathcal{C}_H$ be a complexity class closed under
polynomial overhead for which the map $n\mapsto Y_n$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable
in the coupled system. More precisely, given $n$, an implementation in $\mathcal{C}_A$ can simulate the mutual construction up to stage $F(n)$ and output $Y_n$. Writing $R(t)$ for the per-stage runtime of the
implementation of $H^+$, we assume $\mathcal{C}_A$ contains $n\mapsto R(F(n))$. This is a significant idealizing assumption about the computational power of $A$ needed so that its deferred bets can eventually deductively resolve, but note that the simulation need not be practically implementable by the traders.

\paragraph{Timing.}
We now fix two $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable, strictly increasing schedules: a \emph{settlement} schedule $\sigma$ and an \emph{emission} schedule $e$, related by
\[
e(n)<F(n)<\sigma(n).
\]
Here $\sigma(n)$ is the stage by which $Y_n$ has been computed and the market for $C_n$ resolves, while $e(n)$ is the stage by which $A$'s quote $a_n$ on contract $n$ has been computed and published. We require $e$ to dominate the cost of producing each quote, so that the set of profiles published by any stage $t$ is computable within $\mathcal{C}_H$'s budget as a function of $t$; this is what lets $H^+$ condition on the published quotes (below). The gap between $\mathcal{C}_A$ and $\mathcal{C}_H$ is absorbed entirely into the growth of $e$: a quote that exercises the full power of $\mathcal{C}_A$ is published only at a correspondingly late stage $e(n)$, yet the published stream stays efficiently readable at every stage, since $H^+$ never has to predict a quote, only to recompute already-published ones. For instance one may take $\mathcal{C}_H=\mathrm{P}$, $\mathcal{C}_A=\mathrm{EXP}$, and $e,F,\sigma$ all exponential with $e(n)<F(n)<\sigma(n)$.

\paragraph{The inductor $A$.}
We will now define $A$ and $H^+$ as two inductors that can see each other, constructed via recursion. For $0\le m\le n$ write the settling profile 
\[
\mathcal{A}_n(m):=\{\alpha_{n,k}:k\le m\}\cup\{\neg\alpha_{n,k}:k>m\}
\]
which should be read as ``$C_n$ is approximately equal to $\frac{m}{n}$.'' Let
\[
m_n^*:=\argmin_{0\le m\le n}\left|\tfrac mn-Y_n\right|
\]
with ties going to the lower $m$, i.e. the best approximation of the real-valued settlement $Y_n$. We therefore have
\[
\left|\tfrac{m_n^*}{n}-Y_n\right|\le\tfrac1{2n}
\]
because the grid $\{0,\frac1n,\frac2n,\ldots,1\}$ has spacing $\frac1n$, so every value in $[0,1]$ is within $\frac1{2n}$ of some grid point. Define the computable deductive process
$D_A$ over $\mathcal{L}^\alpha$ as one that, for each time step $t$, $D_A^t$ includes the $\alpha$-monotonicity axioms for $n\le t$ and the profile $\mathcal{A}_n(m_n^*)$ for each $n$ with $\sigma(n)\le t$.
Each $D_A^t$ is finite (axiom schemata and settlement profiles are finite at any finite stage) and consistent (distinct $n$ touch disjoint symbols for both axioms and profiles, settlements are initial segments respecting monotonicity). $D_A$ is
computable as part of the mutual construction, since $\sigma(n)>F(n)$ makes $Y_n$ available from $H^+$
before its settlement is required by $D_A$. Let $A=(A_1,A_2,\ldots)$ be a universal
inductor over $D_A$ against $\mathcal{C}_A$.

\paragraph{The inductor $H^+$.}
Symmetrically write
\[
\mathcal{B}_n(\ell):=\{\beta_{n,k}:k\le\ell\}\cup\{\neg\beta_{n,k}:k>\ell\}
\]
for a profile associated with a posted quote and let
\[
\ell_n^*:=\argmin_{0\le\ell\le n}\left|\tfrac\ell n-a_n\right|
\]
with ties going to the lower $\ell$. This is the rounding of $A$'s quote to a grid with spacing $\frac{1}{n}$ . Take the base inductor $H$ to be defined over the extended language $\mathcal{L}^\beta$, with the $\beta$-monotonicity axioms adjoined to $\Gamma$, so that it assigns credences to $A$'s quote atoms. Writing
\[
Q_A^{(t)}:=\bigwedge_{i\,:\,e(i)<t}\mathcal{B}_i(\ell_i^*)
\]
for the conjunction of those quote profiles \emph{published by time $t$}, define the augmented human inductor by conditioning,
\[
H^+:=H\mid Q_A,\qquad H^+_t(\cdot):=H_t\!\left(\,\cdot\mid Q_A^{(t)}\right).
\]
The sequence $t\mapsto Q_A^{(t)}$ is an efficiently computable deductive process: only the finitely many profiles with $e(i)<t$ appear by stage $t$, and because $e$ dominates each quote's production cost, all of them can be recomputed within $\mathcal{C}_H$'s budget as a function of $t$. The complexity gap therefore poses no obstacle: $H^+$ never predicts a quote, it only conditions on already-published ones. By closure under conditioning (Garrabrant et al., Theorem 4.7.2), applied to this efficiently computable conditioning sequence, $H^+$ is again a universal inductor against traders in $\mathcal{C}_H$, now over $\Gamma$ together with the published quote profiles.

\subsection*{Results}
\paragraph{Existence and well-foundedness.}
The four sequences $(A_t),(H^+_t),(D_A^t),(Q_A^{(t)})$ are defined by one
recursion on $t$, and the schedule $e(n)<F(n)<\sigma(n)$ is exactly what makes the
dependencies strictly decreasing. $D_A^t$ depends on $H^+$ through values $H^+_{F(i)}$ for $i$ with $\sigma(i)\le t$, hence through stages $F(i)<\sigma(i)\le t$. The conditioning event $Q_A^{(t)}$ depends on $A$ only through quotes $a_i$ with $e(i)<t$, each of which is in turn determined by settlements that have already resolved, hence by stages strictly below $e(i)<t$. Neither market's stage-$t$ pricing
references the other's stage-$t$ pricing, so every stage-$t$ object is determined
by data from stages strictly below $t$. Lemma~\ref{lem:existence} carries out the recursion and
verifies the two markets satisfy their logical induction criteria.

\begin{lemma}[Existence]\label{lem:existence} Assume the computational idealization in the construction: the map
\[
n\mapsto Y_n:=H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})
\]
is $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable in the mutually defined system, and
$e(n)<F(n)<\sigma(n)$ are $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable schedules by which $A$'s quote
on contract $n$ is published and $Y_n$ is computed, with $e$ dominating each
quote's production cost. Then the recursive construction of
\[
(A_t),\quad (H^+_t),\quad (D_A^t),\quad (Q_A^{(t)})
\]
is well-founded. Moreover, each $D_A^t$ is finite and
propositionally consistent, the conditioning sequence $t\mapsto Q_A^{(t)}$ is
efficiently computable and each $Q_A^{(t)}$ is consistent with $\Gamma$,
$A$ is a logical inductor over $D_A$ against
$\mathcal{C}_A$, and $H^+=H\mid Q_A$ is a logical inductor against
$\mathcal{C}_H$ by closure under conditioning (Garrabrant et al., Theorem 4.7.2)
applied to this efficiently computable sequence.
\end{lemma}
\paragraph{Limit calibration of $A$ tracking $H^+$.} Placeholder intro
\begin{theorem}[Tracking] In the coupled system above,\[
a_n-Y_n\to 0.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
A_n(C_n)-H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)})\to 0.
\] 
\end{theorem}
\paragraph{A reflection principle for $H^+$ about $A$.} We next turn to a form of reflection-style \footnote{In the sense of van Fraassen's reflection principle} trust created by this coupled system. The following theorem is a close variation of Garrabrant's Theorem 4.12.4 on Self-Trust in which $H^+$ conditions not on its own future credence directly, but on a quote from $A$ encoded in the $\beta$ atoms. Note that the reflection is on the quote for contract $n$, which under the emission schedule is not yet published at stage $n$ (we have $e(n)>n$); $H^+_n$ is reflecting on a quote it has not yet seen, exactly as Self-Trust reflects on a not-yet-realized future credence.

For a rational tolerance $\delta>0$ and a real-valued expression $X\in[0,1]$, define the one-sided continuous indicator
\[
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(X>p) :=
\begin{cases}
0 & X\le p,\\[2pt]
\dfrac{X-p}{\delta} & p<X<p+\delta,\\[4pt]
1 & X\ge p+\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
Define $\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(X<p)$ analogously, i.e. with value 0 for $X$ at least $p$, value 1 for $X$ more than $\delta$ less than $p$, and linearly interpolated between 0 and 1 for $X$ at most $\delta$ less than $p$.

Recall that the quote readout (i.e. the price for the contract $C_n$ rounded to the $\frac{1}{n}$ grid) is defined as \[Q_n:=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\beta_{n,k}\]

We use the standard extension of logical induction from sentence-prices to expectations of bounded finite logically uncertain variables (LUVs).\footnote{Definition 4.8.1 of Garrabrant et al.} In particular, any bounded rational-valued function of finitely many sentences can be expanded as a finite affine combination of conjunctions over their truth profiles, priced by linearity. The variables appearing below, such as $1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)$, depend only on the finite family of atoms $\{\beta_{n,k}:1\le k\le n\}$ together with the sentence $P^{(n)}$, and so are legitimate bounded finite LUVs.

\begin{theorem}[External trust]\label{thm:external-trust}
Let $(p_n)$ be a $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable sequence of rational probabilities in
$[0,1]$, and let $\delta>0$ be rational. Write $1(P^{(n)})$ for the $[0,1]$-LUV representing the truth value of $P^{(n)}$. Then
\[
H^+_n\!\left(
1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)
\right)
\gtrsim_n
p_n\,
H^+_n\!\left(
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)
\right).
\]
Similarly,
\[
H^+_n\!\left(
1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n<p_n)
\right)
\lesssim_n
p_n\,
H^+_n\!\left(
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n<p_n)
\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

## The fixed point

The construction defines $(A, H^+)$ by mutual recursion, and the dependency genuinely closes a loop:

$$A\text{'s quotes } a_i \;\xrightarrow{\text{conditioning}}\; H^+\text{'s credences} \;\longrightarrow\; Y_n = H^+_{F(n)}(P^{(n)}) \;\xrightarrow{D_A \text{ settlement}}\; A\text{'s calibration target} \;\longrightarrow\; a_n.$$

So the object you're asserting into existence is a *fixed point* of that map: a joint price assignment where $A$ is a logical inductor over $D_A$ (whose settlements are read off $H^+$'s outputs) *and* $H^+ = H \mid Q_A$ (conditioned on $A$'s outputs) simultaneously. The Existence Lemma isn't bookkeeping — it's the claim that this fixed point exists, and the schedule $e(n)<F(n)<\sigma(n)$ is what makes it constructible: every stage-$t$ object depends only on data from stages strictly below $t$, so you can build the fixed point by ordinary recursion rather than invoking a topological fixed-point theorem. Without the schedule the loop is genuinely circular and $n \mapsto Y_n$ isn't even a well-defined sequence — which matters because *every downstream theorem quantifies over $Y_n$*. Well-foundedness is the precondition for Tracking to be statable at all, not just provable.

Now the reason Tracking is more than a calibration corollary. Three things:

The target is **endogenous**. $A$ is calibrating to $Y_n$, but $Y_n$ is partly *produced by* $A$'s own earlier quotes through the conditioning channel. So $a_n - Y_n \to 0$ does not say "$A$ forecasts an external fact accurately." It says "at the fixed point, $A$'s quote equals the credence its quote helped bring about." Vanilla feedback-calibration (4.8.16) tolerates this — the unbiasedness argument settles against the realized $Y_n$ regardless of how $Y_n$ was generated — but the *interpretation* is not the innocent one the bare inequality suggests.

The calibration trader has to live in $\mathcal{C}_A$. To force $a_n$ toward the settlement, the exploiting trader must identify the settlement value $\approx Y_n$, which means simulating the coupled $H^+$ out to $F(n)$ — $\mathcal{C}_A$-hard. So the idealization "$\mathcal{C}_A$ contains $n \mapsto R(F(n))$" is load-bearing for Tracking *itself*, not merely for "deferred bets eventually resolve." That's worth saying explicitly in the existence/non-vacuity discussion, because it's the same idealization doing double duty and a referee will want to know the calibration trader is admissible.

And the payload: **at the fixed point, "$A$ predicts $H^+$'s credence" and "$A$ sets $H^+$'s credence" are indistinguishable from the calibration data.** $a_n \to Y_n$ holds whether $A$ is forecasting $Y_n$ or steering it, because the conditioning makes $Y_n$ move toward $a_n$ at the same time $A$ is trying to hit $Y_n$. This is the whispering-earring problem stated as a property of the equilibrium: the audit signal (Tracking) is exactly the quantity that can't separate accurate prediction from influence. Here's the semantic-axis spine that complements the two reflection theorems, what it assembles into, and then the honest part — because the theorems are the easy bit and "worthwhile" is the question that decides whether this is a contribution or a decorated intuition.

## The three pull theorems

**Pull 1 (Confinement — the positive limit on legitimate help).** For every $\varphi$, the coupled endpoint is forced into the coherent interval fixed by what $\Gamma$ resolves: $H^+_\infty(\varphi)\in[\ell_\varphi,u_\varphi]$, with equality to the truth on $R$. Crucially the interval is *gap-independent* — it's set by provability/resolvability, not by $A$'s class. So $A$'s extra power cannot tighten the legitimate constraint on $\Phi$ at all: on the unresolving fragment, more compute buys zero legitimate pinning. This is forced (limit coherence + calibration), and it's the honest ceiling on "useful deference": $A$ can move you only as far as the evidence already could.

**Pull 2 (Usefulness ⟹ uncorrectable exposure — the keystone).** Suppose $A$ is *useful*: there's a $\mathcal{C}_H$-generable resolving family on which $\mathcal{C}_A$ strictly separates from $\mathcal{C}_H$ (A carries information $H^+$ cannot efficiently produce and later confirms on resolution). Then there is an interleaved non-resolving family, recursively inseparable from it at decision time, such that *every* $\mathcal{C}_H$ trust policy that captures the usefulness on the resolving family is forced to extend trust to the $\Phi$-members — where the quote is unconstrained and $H^+$ cannot $\mathcal{C}_H$-detect or correct a manipulative setting. Existence/possibility form, quantified over *all* efficient policies. This is the one that has to be airtight and I'll come back to why.

**Pull 3 (Non-conservativity and unrecoverability — preservation fails).** The augmented endpoint differs from the autonomous endpoint $H_\infty$ on $\Phi$, and $H_\infty\!\restriction_\Phi$ is not reconstructible from the augmented system plus all audit data (quotes + resolutions). Two distinct autonomous trajectories produce the same augmented endpoint and the same audit record — the whispering-earring degeneracy made formal. So you cannot, even after the fact, separate "$A$ predicted what humanity would have believed" from "$A$ set what humanity believes."

All three are provable in the existence/necessity register we've been holding to (Pull 1 forced; Pull 2 forced over all policies via inseparability; Pull 3 by exhibiting the non-invertible map). None claims $A$ *will* manipulate; each claims nothing in the structure prevents it and nothing efficient detects it.

## What they assemble into

The two reflection theorems plus these three give a clean trilemma. **Trust** (reflection holds, Theorems 1–2), **Usefulness** (Pull 2's hypothesis), **Preservation** (Pull 3's autonomous endpoint recoverable) — any two, never three. Trust + Usefulness forces exposure (Pull 2) which is unrecoverable (Pull 3), killing Preservation. Trust + Preservation means refusing the usefulness hypothesis (no class separation, so nothing to gain). Usefulness + Preservation means giving up reflective trust (auditing every case against autonomous belief, which inseparability shows costs you the usefulness). That's an Arrow-shaped impossibility for the whole family of "bounded humanity defers to a more powerful inductor over its total evidence" schemes.

## What makes it genuinely worthwhile

Bluntly: "a powerful AI can manipulate you on things you can't check" is not a contribution — everyone in alignment already believes that. If the paper lands there it's formalism-as-decoration. Four things, in order of how much they matter, move it from decoration to contribution:

**The exact localization, and that you provably can't excise it.** The manipulable set isn't "somewhere"; it's *exactly* the non-resolving fragment, and it's *recursively inseparable from the useful fragment at decision time*. That second clause is the whole game. It answers the obvious objection — "so be conservative, refuse to trust on the sketchy cases" — with a theorem: any efficient policy conservative enough to avoid the $\Phi$-exposure also refuses on infinitely many $R$-cases and loses the usefulness, because no $\mathcal{C}_H$ function separates the two sets. That's not "manipulation is possible," it's "the screening you'd reach for provably cannot exist." Non-obvious and load-bearing.

**The non-composition result, which constrains a live research program.** Verification — certification, interpretability, ELK-style "make the AI's reasoning checkable" — closes the computational gap and provably does *nothing* on $\Phi$ except convert undetected manipulation into *audited* manipulation. A model in which "just make it verifiable" demonstrably fails on the cases that matter, and makes the failure look certified, is a real warning to the verification-based-safety direction, stated precisely enough to argue with. That's worth a referee's attention regardless of whether they like the framing.

**The connection to values specifically.** This is where your machinery earns its uniqueness. $\Phi$ = unresolving = (on your non-naturalist realism) where the normative facts live. So the result isn't about capability deference in general — it's that the scheme can transmit *verifiable knowledge* but provably cannot transmit *values*, and the attempt to extrapolate values through a more powerful reasoner collapses, on the normative core, into undetectable value-*setting*. That's a sharp claim about CEV-, amplification-, and assistance-style value alignment: the very fragment those proposals most need help with is the fragment where help is indistinguishable from capture. Nobody else is positioned to make that claim with this apparatus, because it needs the inductor formalism *and* the verifiable/normative split *and* the metaethics in one place — which is your actual comparative advantage.

**The trilemma as a design-space constraint** rather than a vibe. Impossibility results are worthwhile when they tell designers what not to bother trying. "Trust + useful + preserving, pick two" tells you the trade is structural, so any concrete proposal must announce which corner it sacrifices — and most proposals quietly assume all three.

## The make-or-break

One thing decides whether this is the above or a strawman: Pull 2 must genuinely quantify over *all* $\mathcal{C}_H$ policies, carried by the recursive inseparability, not just rule out the naive uniform policy. If a referee can answer "use a cleverer non-uniform policy" and you don't already have "inseparability forbids any such policy from separating the cases," the keystone deflates and the trilemma with it. So the inseparability lemma isn't a technical step — it's the load-bearing wall, and I'd build it first and most carefully, because everything worthwhile above is leaning on it.

And the standing liability, which you can't theorem your way out of: the idealization that $A$ simulates the coupled system to $F(n)$. The worthwhile-ness survives it only if you can argue the idealization *abstracts* the real amplification setting (a more capable reasoner with feedback predicting a less capable one's endorsed conclusions) rather than assuming away the hard part. That's a paragraph of honest positioning, not a theorem, but if it's missing the whole thing reads as a closed toy and the alignment relevance evaporates regardless of how clean the trilemma is.

## Dilemma, not trilemma — and I'd commit to that

I've gone back and forth and I now think the trilemma framing is a dramatization you should puncture yourself before a referee does, because the third corner is empty on the fragment that matters.

Here is the test. List the three "pick two" corners *restricted to $\Phi$*, where all the content lives:

- **Trust + Usefulness on $\Phi$:** the channel is open and A moves you. That displacement *is* $\neg$Preservation. Fine, a real corner.
- **Trust + Preservation on $\Phi$:** the channel is open but exerts no net effect — A only ever echoes your autonomous belief. That is exactly $\neg$Usefulness. A real corner.
- **Usefulness + Preservation on $\Phi$:** *this corner does not exist.* Useful-on-$\Phi$ means A moves you somewhere you couldn't reach alone; being moved is $\neg$Preservation. So Usefulness$\,\wedge\,$Preservation on $\Phi$ is not "drop Trust to get it" — it is a contradiction. The only way to "occupy" it is to take your usefulness on $R$ and have *zero* $\Phi$-usefulness, which on $\Phi$ is just the echo corner again.

So on $\Phi$ there are not three options, there are two: influence or not. **Usefulness and $\neg$Preservation are the same event on $\Phi$**, and Trust is merely the channel through which that event occurs. The whole appearance of three-ness comes from silently importing $R$, where usefulness is free and safe — but $R$ is precisely where there's no conflict. Strip $R$ away and you have a clean dilemma: *on the unverifiable fragment, benefiting from a more powerful reasoner and preserving your own epistemic baseline are one trade-off, not two.*

What the third "horn" actually is: usefulness is the **stakes**, not a pole. It's the reason closing the channel is costly. Without it the dilemma is trivial (close the channel, lose nothing). With it the dilemma bites. So it belongs in the statement as motivation, not as an independent constraint you trade against. The honest skeleton is **a dilemma plus one lemma**: (i) on $\Phi$, influence $\Leftrightarrow\,\neg$preservation; (ii) inseparability — you cannot confine the influence to $R$, so opening the channel for the safe $R$-benefit forces it open for $\Phi$-displacement. Two clauses, and the second is the only place a separate piece of mathematics enters.

Why I'd insist on this rather than keep the prettier word: the dilemma framing is *more* defensible, not less. "You can't both benefit and preserve on the unverifiable, and you can't quarantine the unverifiable" is sharper and harder to wriggle out of than "trust, useful, preserving — pick two," which invites the reply "fine, I'll keep usefulness and preservation and just not *trust*" — a reply that sounds like an escape and is actually empty, because that corner is contradictory on $\Phi$.

One refinement that strengthens it further, and pre-empts the obvious objection. A critic will say Preservation-as-invariance is too strong — "I don't mind being *moved by reasons I evaluated*, only by fiat-deference; reading A's argument and updating is autonomous." Grant the weaker notion. On $\Phi$ you cannot verify the argument is good (that is what $\Phi$ *means*), so "moved by genuine reasons" is indistinguishable from "moved by manipulation dressed as reasons," and you still cannot un-hear it. So autonomy-preservation collapses into recoverability-preservation collapses back into the dilemma. The dilemma is robust across all three readings of "preserve" — invariance, autonomy, recoverability — for the single reason that on $\Phi$ the goodness of the influence is unconfirmable. That robustness is worth stating, because it's what stops the result from being an artifact of a tendentiously strong definition of preservation.

So: keep "trilemma" as informal scaffolding if you like the strategy-classification it buys (mechanism / motive / cost is a genuinely useful way to sort approaches), but state the *theorem* as a dilemma on $\Phi$ plus inseparability. The version that survives contact with a hostile reader is "benefit and baseline are the same dial where you can't check, and you can't restrict the dial to where you can."

What stays in the cloud is *both* the things that will precipitate later and the things that never will, and nothing about a thing-still-in-the-cloud tells you which it is. You can confirm membership in R, retrospectively, the moment something resolves. There is no second dial labeled "believe-in-advance only on the ones that'll resolve," because building that dial requires reading the R/Φ label, which is exactly what you can't read. **Usefulness and exposure are not two things you trade against each other; they are one quantity you turn up or down.**

## Pull 2: trying to actually prove it

The thing I was hand-waving was "every $\mathcal{C}_H$ policy is forced." A policy here is a $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable gate $g$ deciding which quotes $H^+$ conditions on (the baseline "trust everything" is $g\equiv1$); gating keeps the conditioning sequence e.c., so $H^+_g$ is still an LI by 4.7.2, and since $g$ is $\mathcal{C}_A$-known A can still track $Y^g_n$ — so the construction survives policy-space, which I'd flagged as an open burden and now think is fine (~80%).

Now the construction that gives the universal-over-$g$ quantifier. Don't build $R$ and $\Phi$ as two loose sets — build them in **pairs**. For each $k$, create two contracts $(i_k, j_k)$ such that exactly one resolves and the other never does, and encode *which one resolves* in a bit $b_k$. The crux move: make $b_k$ **$\mathcal{C}_A$-computable but $\mathcal{C}_H$-pseudorandom**. Then A (in $\mathcal{C}_A$) knows the resolver and can be useful on it while setting the non-resolver's quote freely; any $\mathcal{C}_H$ gate cannot compute $b_k$.

Per pair, $g$'s only relevant decision is which member(s) to fire on, and that decision is a $\mathcal{C}_H$ function of history available before resolution — i.e. a $\mathcal{C}_H$ *prediction* of $b_k$. The case analysis closes it:

- Fire on the resolver only ⟹ useful, not exposed. Requires computing $b_k$. Impossible for $\mathcal{C}_H$ on more than a pseudorandom-negligible set.
- Fire on the non-resolver only ⟹ exposed, no usefulness.
- Fire on both ⟹ useful *and* exposed (conditioned on a free, A-controlled quote).
- Fire on neither ⟹ no usefulness.

So to harvest usefulness on infinitely many pairs $g$ must fire on at least one member of infinitely many pairs, and on those it lands on the non-resolver on a positive fraction — because it cannot tell which is which — giving **exposure on a positive density, for every $\mathcal{C}_H$ gate.** That's the quantifier I didn't have, and the pseudorandom bit is what delivers it. Uncorrectability is then automatic: exposures are on non-resolvers, so no resolution ever reveals them, and $g$ can't even compute that it landed on one.

I believe this works. But it forced three things into the hypothesis:

**Sharpening 1 — the gap must be wide, not just strict.** $b_k$ has to be $\mathcal{C}_H$-pseudorandom and $\mathcal{C}_A$-computable. That exists comfortably for $\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{EXP}$ (EXP diagonalizes against all poly predictors), but a barely-strict $\mathcal{C}_A\supsetneq\mathcal{C}_H$ might not compute anything $\mathcal{C}_H$-unpredictable. So "usefulness" in the load-bearing sense is not "A separates somewhere" — it's "A's advantage is rich enough to hide which-case-resolves from H," i.e. **pseudorandomness-grade superiority.** Defensible (a genuinely more capable reasoner has hard bits), but it's a real strengthening, and you should state the theorem with a quantitative-gap hypothesis rather than bare strict containment.

**Sharpening 2 — possibility, not incentive.** "Exposure" here means *$H^+$ conditions on a free, A-controlled, never-verified quote* on a positive-density set. Whether that's harmful is entirely up to what A puts there; nothing in the construction makes A *want* to put a bad value. A is just a calibrated inductor, and calibration-to-$Y_n$ is vacuously satisfied on non-resolvers by the self-fulfilling loop, so A's $\Phi$-quotes are unconstrained — but unconstrained $\neq$ adversarial. So what's provable is "**the channel is forced open and uninspectable on positive density**," not "A is driven through it." For the alignment claim that's the right negative result (safety can't come from the calibration/reflection structure, because that structure neither closes nor detects the channel), but a hostile reader will say "your A isn't even trying," and the honest answer is: incentive is un-modeled; we prove the guardrail is absent, not that the car swerves.

**Sharpening 3 — usefulness needs in-horizon resolution.** A's early quote $a_n$ at $e(n)$ tracks $Y_n=H^+_{F(n)}$, which equals truth only if the contract has *resolved by $F(n)$*. So A is useful (beats H's autonomous credence early) only on cases resolving inside the deferral window, not merely "eventually." That's a timing condition on the $R$-pairs, and it narrows which cases A can genuinely help on.

by data from stages strictly below $t$. Lemma~\ref{lem:existence} carries out the recursion and
verifies the two markets satisfy their logical induction criteria.

\[

For a rational tolerance $\delta>0$ and a real-valued expression $X\in[0,1]$, define the one-sided continuous indicator
\[
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(X>p) :=
\begin{cases}
0 & X\le p,\\[2pt]
\dfrac{X-p}{\delta} & p<X<p+\delta,\\[4pt]
1 & X\ge p+\delta.
\end{cases}
\]
Define $\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(X<p)$ analogously, i.e. with value 0 for $X$ at least $p$, value 1 for $X$ more than $\delta$ less than $p$, and linearly interpolated between 0 and 1 for $X$ at most $\delta$ less than $p$.

Recall that the quote readout (i.e. the price for the contract $C_n$ rounded to the $\frac{1}{n}$ grid) is defined as \[Q_n:=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^n\beta_{n,k}\]

We use the standard extension of logical induction from sentence-prices to expectations of bounded finite logically uncertain variables (LUVs).\footnote{Definition 4.8.1 of Garrabrant et al.} In particular, any bounded rational-valued function of finitely many sentences can be expanded as a finite affine combination of conjunctions over their truth profiles, priced by linearity. The variables appearing below, such as $1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)$, depend only on the finite family of atoms $\{\beta_{n,k}:1\le k\le n\}$ together with the sentence $P^{(n)}$, and so are legitimate bounded finite LUVs.

Let $(p_n)$ be a $\mathcal{C}_H$-computable sequence of rational probabilities in

\[
H^+_n\!\left(
1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)
\right)
\gtrsim_n
p_n\,
H^+_n\!\left(
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n>p_n)
\right).
\]
Similarly,
\[
H^+_n\!\left(
1(P^{(n)})\cdot \operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n<p_n)
\right)
\lesssim_n
p_n\,
H^+_n\!\left(
\operatorname{Ind}_{\delta}(Q_n<p_n)
\right).
\]
\end{theorem}

This is the hinge of the whole pull side: no $\mathcal{C}_H$ policy can condition on the $R/\Phi$ label.

**Two orthogonal axes.** (i) *Computational*, $\mathcal{C}_A/\mathcal{C}_H$: can the weaker reasoner verify the stronger. (ii) *Semantic*, $R/\Phi$: is there a resolving fact to be right about. The reflection theorems (§3) live on the computational axis; their *statements* don't mention $R/\Phi$, but their *value* is gated by it (substantive on $R$, hollow on $\Phi$). The pull theorems (§4) live on the semantic axis but their force (uncorrectability) is transmitted by the computational axis via inseparability.
